newsitem.title: INDIA: Sikh party poised to win in India's Punjab state.
newsitem.headline: Sikh party poised to win in India's Punjab state.

text.p: A pro-Sikh regional party headed for an absolute majority on Sunday in key local polls in India's northern state of Punjab, promising religious harmony and a durable rule with its Hindu nationalist ally, officials said.

They said the predominantly Sikh Akali Dal party of former state chief minister Prakash Singh Badal had won 13 seats in the 117-member state assembly and was leading comfortably in another 54 in results and trends available at 8.30 pm (1500 GMT).
"The Akali Dal is cruising to a comfortable majority," Punjab's chief election official Brajendra Singh told Reuters in the state capital of Chandigarh,
The ruling Congress party which won 87 seats in the 1992 state polls was leading in 13 constituencies with only one declared win so far, he said.
India's main opposition rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), junior ally of the Dal in Punjab, had won three races and was well ahead in 15 other constituencies, Singh said.
The results spurred hopes of peace in the troubled state.
Akali Dal's former interior minister Kanwaljit Singh told Reuters his party had shifted its focus from the welfare of the state's majority Sikhs to friendship with Punjab's Hindus.

"Hindus may be in a minority in Punjab, but we have realised that the state cannot progress without their total involvement in its governance," Kanwaljit Singh said as news trickled in of the Akali Dal's resounding victory.
Election officials began counting votes early on Sunday amid tight security across the state. Results were expected to be announced by late evening.
More than 68 percent of Punjab's 15 million voters turned out on Friday in a remarkably peaceful election for the state assembly. The turnout was earlier estimated at 65 percent.
"The combination will get 100 seats of which 15 will belong to the BJP," said Kanwaljit Singh.
The BJP is contesting 22 seats while Akali Dal has put up candidates in 92 constituencies. Three other candidates were being backed by both.

The polls for the state assembly were the first in two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatist violence. Officials said, however, that the state's political groups were too badly divided to ensure badly-needed stability.
But Sukbhir Grewal, an independent political analyst, said: "There is no reason to believe that the Akali Dal will do anything to retard the peace prcess in Punjab."
The Akali Dal's poll alliance with BJP was seen as offering a chance to Punjab's two main communities -- Hindus and Sikhs -- to heal their mistrust, analysts said.
"These elections will prove to be a triumph for Punjabi unity," said Balramji Das Tandon, a BJP candidate in the Rajpura constitency.
Punjab's ruling Congress party, led by the state's first woman chief minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, claims credit for the virtual weeding out of Sikh militancy from the region.
Sikh separatist violence peaked after Indian troops were sent into the Golden Temple in Amritsar in 1984 to flush out militants holed up in the Sikhs' holiest shrine.
Then-prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in what was believed to be a revenge killing for the army assault.
The state polls in 1992, which revived local democracy after more than a decade of separatist violence, took place in an atmosphere of fear and overwhelming security.
